\chapter{Five Places and Things in a Week}
\label{ch:la-universidad-y-el-trabajo}
\hlchaptermodality{394}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say la universidad, el trabajo, la actividad, la guitarra and el médico, and name five places I go or things I do in a week.}

Complete ES-C394-medico: name five places I go or things I do in a week, and say one thing about each.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[la universidad]{la universidad — a body of people, before it was a place}

\label{lesson:ES-C394-universidad}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the address}, then \emph{the nationality}. (\emph{La dirección}; \emph{La nacionalidad}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el estudiante — who the word was named after.
  \item la escuela — the other place you go to learn.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{u-ni-ver-si-DAD}, five beats with the weight on the last. The opening \emph{u} is \emph{oo}, not the English \emph{you-}. The \emph{v} comes out as a \emph{b}. The \emph{s} stays a clean hiss, and the final \emph{d} is soft, nearer the \emph{th} of \emph{the}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la universidad} — \textquotedblleft{}university.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{ūniversitās} — and the meaning to hold onto is not the one the shape tempts you into. In Roman and medieval law a \emph{ūniversitās} was a \textbf{body of people}: a corporation, a guild, a company treated as one thing. A trade guild was a \emph{universitas}. So was a town council.

A medieval university got its name the same way — after the people in it, not after the breadth of what they studied. On the exact phrase the references part company. Corominas shortens it from \emph{universitas scholarium}, the guild of students. Etymonline gives \emph{universitas magistrorum et scholarium}, of masters and students. Take the shape and leave the sentence: what got named was an association of its members.

The pieces: \textbf{ūnus}, one, plus \textbf{versus}, the turned form of \textbf{vertere}, to turn. \emph{Ūniversus} is \emph{turned into one}, many things faced the same way. English holds that in \textbf{universe} and \textbf{universal}; \emph{vertere} alone hands over \textbf{verse}, \textbf{version}, \textbf{convert}, \textbf{reverse}, \textbf{divorce} and \textbf{vertigo}.

Two dates carry the argument better than any reasoning could.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1490}, Alfonso de Palencia — the earliest Spanish \emph{universidad} on record. It means \textbf{totality}, the whole of a thing. No school in sight.
  \item \textbf{1505} — the school sense appears, and cannot stand on its own. What was written is \emph{universidad de estudio}, a \emph{universidad} \textbf{of study}.
\end{itemize}

That second date is the tell. A word already meaning \textquotedblleft{}the whole of knowledge\textquotedblright{} would have needed no such help.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name where you study: \emph{la universidad}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la universidad}
  \item \emph{estudio en la universidad}
  \item \emph{la universidad es grande}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What kind of thing was a Latin \emph{ūniversitās}? (A body of people — a corporation or guild, held together as one.) And what did the first Spanish \emph{universidad}, in 1490, mean? (Totality. The school sense came fifteen years later, needing the phrase \emph{universidad de estudio} to say so.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el trabajo]{el trabajo — a word with an asterisk in the middle of it}

\label{lesson:ES-C394-trabajo}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the nationality}, then \emph{the university}. (\emph{La nacionalidad}; \emph{La universidad}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item trabajar — the doing word this is cut from.
  \item la semana — the stretch you measure it in.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tra-BA-jo}, three beats with the weight on the middle one. The \emph{r} is one quick tap of the tongue, not the English glide. The \emph{b} between vowels is soft, the lips never quite closing. The \emph{j} is the throaty \emph{jota}, scraped at the back. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el trabajo} — \textquotedblleft{}work\textquotedblright{}; also \textquotedblleft{}a job\textquotedblright{}, and a piece of work you hand in.

Corominas dates it in Spanish to \textbf{1212}. Behind it sits Vulgar Latin \textbf{tripaliāre}, \textquotedblleft{}to torture\textquotedblright{}, on Late Latin \textbf{tripalium}, an instrument of torture. Told properly it has an asterisk in the middle, and the asterisk is where the honesty lives.

\textbf{The instrument is real.} \emph{Tripalium} is on record, spelled \textbf{trepalium}, in the Councils of Auxerre and Mâcon. The Auxerre canon of \textbf{578} forbids a priest or deacon to stand \emph{ad trepalium, ubi rei torquentur} — at the \emph{trepalium}, where the accused are tortured. Somebody wrote that down because it stood in a real place.

\emph{\textbf{Tripaliāre\emph{ is not.\textbf{ The form that would mean \textquotedblleft{}to torture with one\textquotedblright{} carries an asterisk in the Academy's dictionary and in Corominas alike: reconstructed backwards from its descendants, because no surviving text holds it. Two claims, two grades of evidence, worth keeping apart.}}}}

What saves the story from being a good line is that the middle of it is documented too:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Old Spanish \emph{trabajo} — \textbf{suffering, pain};
  \item Old Spanish \emph{trabajarse} — \textbf{to strive};
  \item the \textbf{labour} sense — only from the \textbf{fourteenth century};
  \item and the Academy today still carries a sense \emph{penalidad, molestia, tormento}.
\end{itemize}

Torture, suffering, striving, work. Nobody had to guess a link.

One step further up goes soft. \emph{Tripalium} from \textbf{tripalis}, \textquotedblleft{}having three stakes\textquotedblright{}, is called darkly suggestive with its exact notion obscure. Hedge the three stakes; the descent of \emph{trabajo} itself stands.

And refuse the moral. None of this says how Spanish speakers feel about Monday. English \textbf{travail} is the same word, \textbf{travel} its doublet, and nobody calls a holiday agony.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name what you do for a living: \emph{el trabajo}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el trabajo}
  \item \emph{voy al trabajo}
  \item \emph{el trabajo y la universidad}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which part of the story is attested and which is reconstructed? (\emph{Trepalium} is written down in a canon of 578; \textbf{tripaliāre} carries an asterisk in both the Academy and Corominas.) And what did \emph{trabajo} mean in Old Spanish? (Suffering, pain — the work sense only from the fourteenth century.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la actividad]{la actividad — the cluster that never wore down}

\label{lesson:ES-C394-actividad}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the university}, then \emph{the work}. (\emph{La universidad}; \emph{El trabajo}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item hacer — what you do with one.
  \item la clase — where you will meet the word most often.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ac-ti-vi-DAD}, four beats with the weight on the last. The \emph{c} is a hard \emph{k}, and it lands — \emph{k} and \emph{t} back to back. The \emph{t} is dental, tongue against the teeth rather than the ridge behind them. The \emph{v} comes out as a \emph{b}, and the final \emph{d} is soft. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la actividad} — \textquotedblleft{}activity\textquotedblright{}: something you do, and the state of being at it.

Latin \textbf{agere} was to drive, to set in motion, to do. From it \textbf{āctīvus}, and from that \textbf{āctīvitās}. English carries the root in \textbf{activity}, \textbf{active}, \textbf{act}, \textbf{agent}, \textbf{agile}, \textbf{exact} and \textbf{agenda}.

Now the part worth stopping on, because the word wears its own history on the outside. Put these three beside each other and look at the middle:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{factum} $\to$ \textbf{hecho}
  \item \emph{lactem} $\to$ \textbf{leche}
  \item \emph{āctīvitās} $\to$ \textbf{actividad}
\end{itemize}

Two of those went down through mouths for centuries and came out with their \emph{-ct-} rubbed into a \emph{-ch-}. The third still has both letters, and you can still hear both of them land. It did not travel that road; it was lifted off a written page long after the wearing had stopped.

Do not try to argue the same thing from the \emph{-dad} ending — it proves nothing. Words that did come down by mouth arrive at \emph{-dad} as well: \emph{bonitātem} gives \textbf{bondad}. The ending is silent about which road a word took. The cluster is the witness.

Two cautions about the Latin, and neither is small.

\textbf{āctīvitās is not Cicero's word.} It is Medieval Latin, coined by the Scholastics for their own arguments. Writing it out with Classical macrons, as above, flatters it into an age it never had.

\textbf{And the last stretch is dark.} Whether Spanish took \emph{actividad} straight off the Latin page or through French \emph{activité} is unverified. The root is certain, the arrival is not.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name a thing you do with your time: \emph{la actividad}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la actividad}
  \item \emph{una actividad nueva}
  \item \emph{hago una actividad}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What happened to the \emph{-ct-} of \emph{factum} and \emph{lactem}, and what happened to the one in \emph{activ-}? (The first two wore down to \emph{-ch-} in \emph{hecho} and \emph{leche}; \emph{activ-} kept both letters, because it came off the page.) Does the \emph{-dad} ending help you tell? (No — \emph{bonitātem} reaches \emph{bondad} by mouth.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la guitarra]{la guitarra — one Greek word, three disputed roads}

\label{lesson:ES-C394-guitarra}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the work}, then \emph{the activity}. (\emph{El trabajo}; \emph{La actividad}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item tocar — what you do to one.
  \item la cuerda — what it is strung with.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{gui-TA-rra}, three beats with the weight on the middle one. The \emph{gu} before an \emph{i} is a hard \emph{g} and nothing more — \emph{ghee}, not \emph{gwee}; the \emph{u} sits there to keep the \emph{g} hard and is not pronounced. The \emph{t} is dental. The \emph{rr} is rolled, held a moment longer than a tap. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la guitarra} — \textquotedblleft{}guitar.\textquotedblright{}

It starts in Ancient Greek: \textbf{kithára}, \emph{kithára}, a stringed instrument — not this one, but an ancestor of the idea. Its first documented Spanish use is in Juan Ruiz, and it is a fine entrance: he already needs two kinds side by side, \emph{guitarra morisca} and \emph{guitarra latina}.

Between the Greek and the Spanish, the references stop agreeing. This is one of those words where the honest answer is the disagreement itself.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{The Academy's dictionary} takes it from an \textbf{Arabic} form, and that from an \textbf{Aramaic} one, and that from the Greek.
  \item \textbf{Corominas} has the Arabic form coming \textbf{straight from Greek} — no Aramaic step at all; that step is the Academy's addition. And he places the borrowing \textbf{in the East, not by way of Spain}: \emph{el vocablo no pasó de Europa a los árabes por España}. His evidence sits inside the word — the Greek accentuation survives, and so does the hard \emph{k} at the front.
  \item \textbf{Etymonline} routes it through \textbf{French} and Latin \textbf{cithara} with \textbf{no Arabic step whatever}, and adds the sting: the Arabic word may itself have come \emph{from} Spanish or Greek, the relationship often being stated the other way round.
\end{itemize}

That last one does not only doubt the route. It doubts which direction the word was travelling.

So hold the Greek and let the middle stay open. What nobody argues about is the family that came out the far end. English \textbf{guitar}, \textbf{cithara}, \textbf{zither}, \textbf{cittern} and \textbf{gittern} are one Greek word wearing five coats, and Spanish keeps \textbf{cítara} and \textbf{cítola} standing beside \emph{guitarra}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name the instrument: \emph{la guitarra}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la guitarra}
  \item \emph{toco la guitarra}
  \item \emph{tocar la guitarra es una actividad}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which part of the \emph{guitarra} story is settled and which is not? (The Greek \emph{kithára} is settled; the road after it is disputed — the Academy through Arabic and Aramaic, Corominas through Arabic with no Aramaic, and etymonline through French with no Arabic at all, doubting even the direction.) What does the \emph{u} in \emph{gui-} do? (Keeps the \emph{g} hard. It is not pronounced.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el médico]{el médico — three beats that never wore down}

\label{lesson:ES-C394-medico}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the activity}, then \emph{the guitar}. (\emph{La actividad}; \emph{La guitarra}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el hospital — where you find one.
  \item la cita — what you make to see one.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{MÉ-di-co}, three beats with the weight right back on the first, which is what the written mark over the \emph{e} is there to do. The \emph{d} between vowels is soft, nearer the \emph{th} of \emph{the}. The \emph{c} is a hard \emph{k}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el médico} — \textquotedblleft{}doctor\textquotedblright{}: the person, and the profession.

Latin \textbf{medicus}, a physician, from \textbf{medeor}, to heal. English holds the family in \textbf{medic}, \textbf{medical}, \textbf{medicine} and \textbf{remedy}.

What is interesting about \emph{médico} is how little happened to it. Count what survived: three beats, all present; a \emph{d} still between its vowels; a \emph{c} still landing as a hard stop. Nothing worn off anywhere.

Set it against a word that did go down through mouths. Catalan inherited the same \emph{medicus} by ordinary descent and came out with \textbf{metge} — middle beat gone, the hard \emph{c} softened. Occitan \textbf{mètge} and archaic French \textbf{mège} show the same wear. \emph{Médico} has none of it: lifted off a written page instead, late and intact.

An older root sits behind \emph{medeor}, independently supported by \textbf{modus}, \textbf{moderate} and \textbf{meditate}. Take care with it: glossing that root as \textquotedblleft{}measure\textquotedblright{} and then offering a doctor's judgement as proof argues in a circle. The conclusion was smuggled into the gloss.

One thing to hear rather than be told. These three aloud, one after another:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{médico}
  \item \textbf{medico}
  \item \textbf{medicó}
\end{itemize}

Same letters, three different words: the doctor, then \emph{I medicate}, then \emph{he medicated}. Nothing changed but where the weight landed — and the written mark moved with it.

\emph{Médico} does double duty: it names the person, and describes what belongs to the profession — \emph{un centro médico}, a medical centre.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name the doctor: \emph{el médico}. And with it, five places you go or things you do in a week.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el médico}
  \item \emph{voy al médico}
\end{itemize}

Now all five together. Name five places you go or things you do in a week, and say one thing about each.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la universidad — estudio en la universidad}
  \item \emph{el trabajo — voy al trabajo}
  \item \emph{la actividad — hago una actividad nueva}
  \item \emph{la guitarra — toco la guitarra}
  \item \emph{el médico — tengo una cita con el médico}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does Catalan \emph{metge} show that \emph{médico} does not? (Wear — a lost middle beat and a softened \emph{c}; \emph{médico} came off the page intact.) And what separates \emph{médico}, \emph{medico} and \emph{medicó}? (Only where the weight lands.)
\end{tcolorbox}
